linkages: Survey responses linked to administrative records at the individual level (invitations were sent through Denmark's official digital government mailing system)

Respondents assigned to demographic cells defined from register data on seven characteristics (14,112 cells, reduced to 7,362 cells with at least 30 register observations, covering 95.5% of the underlying population of re-employed job seekers)
Respondents linked to jobnet.dk click data and to registered applications (joblog)

sample.universe: All individuals registered as unemployment benefit recipients in Denmark as of 23 October 2023 (all UI beneficiaries and social assistance recipients deemed fit for full-time work by their caseworker), 83,563 in the population benchmark of Table 1
sample.unit_of_observation: individual survey respondent linked to administrative records
selection_rules: All registered benefit recipients invited via the official digital government mailing system; reminder after one week; survey open about five weeks
13,234 individuals completed the main survey (response rate 15.8%)

Respondents who had already accepted a job, sought only part-time work, had never been employed, or belonged to a population cell with fewer than 30 observations in the register data were directed to a shortened survey and excluded from the experiment
Respondents in the top and bottom percentiles of response time in the main survey were dropped
Final sample of 9,247 respondents (4,628 treated, 4,619 control); 3,912 also completed the follow-up survey (3,903 in the balance table)
A separate additional survey was fielded in April and May 2025 to a fresh random sample of 8,000 UI recipients, yielding 902 complete responses
sample.period: Main survey from 23 October 2023 (open about five weeks), follow-up one to two weeks later; administrative outcomes up to six months after the survey; additional survey April-May 2025
sample.n_observations: 9,247 main-survey respondents; 3,912 follow-up respondents; 902 additional-survey respondents; 1,448,020 register observations in Table A.1

construction_notes: Wage projections: average monthly re-employment wages before taxes and excluding pension contributions within each demographic cell, computed from Danish labor market registers covering all unemployed job seekers re-employed between 2013 and 2022; cells defined by age (<=35, 36-50, >50), gender, education (3), previous hours (10-29, >=30), unemployment duration (7 bins), previous monthly salary (ten brackets for full-time, six for part-time) and previous industry (7); 14,112 cells reduced to 7,362 with at least 30 observations

Perception gap: log difference between the actual average re-employment wage of comparable workers and the respondent's prior belief about it; five groups: < -0.15, [-0.15,-0.025), [-0.025,+0.025], (+0.025,+0.15], > +0.15

Subjective wage expectations and all other wage-related outcome variables winsorized at the 5th and 95th percentiles; search intensity and cumulative earnings and working hours winsorized at the 95th percentile

Subjective wage offer distribution elicited over five bins centred on the previous wage (below 80%, 80-95%, 95-105%, 105-120%, above 120%); means and standard deviations computed by assigning midpoints to the inner bins and 72.5% and 127.5% of the previous wage to the outer bins

Prior search radius: average commuting distance between openings applied to in the four weeks before the survey and the place of residence; 'local' below and 'distant' above ten kilometres (roughly the average radius of Danish municipalities)
Anchoring regressions partial out the log pre-unemployment wage (equation 3) to remove mechanical correlation
Lee (2009) bounds for the hourly-wage comparison obtained by trimming the wage distribution of the group with higher employment

claims.statement: Among main-survey respondents with a large positive prior perception gap (log) in (+0.150;+infinity], the randomized provision of information on the actual average re-employment wage of comparable workers (a large positive information shock (the signal exceeds the prior belief by more than 15%)) changes Expected wage offered (log).

treatment.label: Information treatment: randomized provision of the actual average monthly re-employment wage of comparable workers (large positive prior perception gap (log) > +0.15 (initially highly pessimistic))

register_source.value: Danish labor market registers covering all unemployed job seekers re-employed between 2013 and 2022, used to compute the cell-level wage projection; no register code or variable name is stated

definition.value: Binary indicator for being in the randomly selected half of main-survey respondents who were shown, in text and in a bar chart, the actual average monthly re-employment wage (before taxes, excluding pension contributions) of job seekers in their own demographic cell; the control group received no information. The effect is estimated separately within each prior-perception-gap group, so in this group the treatment delivers a large positive information shock (the signal exceeds the prior belief by more than 15%).

timing.value: Delivered during the main online survey (fielded from 23 October 2023), after elicitation of prior beliefs about comparable workers' re-employment wages and before elicitation of expected wage offers, reservation wages and search outcomes

definition.value: Respondent's point estimate of the monthly salary (before taxes, excluding pension contributions) they expect to be offered if offered a full-time job within the next four weeks, in logs; winsorized at the 5th and 95th percentiles

timing.value: Elicited in the main survey, immediately after the information treatment

units.value: log monthly wage offer (DKK)

magnitude.interpretation: raise their wage offer expectations by about 5.2% (p < 0.001)

estimand.target_population: Main-survey respondents with a large positive prior perception gap (log) in (+0.150;+infinity], i.e. job seekers who initially underestimated the average re-employment wage of comparable workers by more than 15% (initially highly pessimistic)
estimand.time_horizon: Measured in the main survey, immediately after the treatment
estimand.formal_query: E[Expected wage offered (log) | do(information provided)] - E[Expected wage offered (log) | do(no information)] for respondents with a large positive prior perception gap (log) > +0.15 (initially highly pessimistic)

population.description: Main-survey respondents with a large positive prior perception gap (log) in (+0.150;+infinity], i.e. job seekers who initially underestimated the average re-employment wage of comparable workers by more than 15% (initially highly pessimistic); N = 1,723 in this estimation
population.ages: Working-age unemployment benefit recipients (age groups: 35 or below, 36-50, above 50)
population.period: Main survey fielded from 23 October 2023 for about five weeks; administrative outcomes followed up to six months after the survey
subgroups_defined: pre-treatment search radius below vs. above ten kilometres (local vs. distant job seekers)
population.selection: Voluntary respondents to a survey invitation sent through Denmark's official digital government mailing system to all registered unemployment benefit recipients as of 23 October 2023 (13,234 completed the main survey, a 15.8% response rate); respondents who had already accepted a job, sought only part-time work, had never been employed or belonged to a register cell with fewer than 30 observations were excluded, as were the top and bottom percentiles of response time

identification.source_of_variation: Random assignment of a random half of main-survey respondents to receive information on the actual average monthly re-employment wage of job seekers in their own demographic cell (survey information-provision experiment fielded from 23 October 2023)

key_assumptions.assumption: Random assignment of the information treatment: within each prior-belief group, treatment status is independent of respondents' potential outcomes and background characteristics, so the treatment-control difference identifies the causal effect of receiving the wage information
key_assumptions.supported_by: Balance tests in Table 1 (treatment-control p-values and joint F-tests of 0.90 for the main and 0.76 for the follow-up sample); Appendix Table A.2 reports characteristics by perception-gap group

rhs: Potential outcomes and baseline characteristics of the respondent

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference between respondents: one respondent's treatment status does not affect another respondent's search behaviour or labour market outcomes (no crowding-out in the vacancy market)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Not tested; the paper notes that assessing the welfare implications of a large-scale roll-out would require accounting for general-equilibrium effects

key_assumptions.assumption: Job seekers regard the re-employment wages of comparable workers as informative for their own wage prospects (the design's explicitly testable assumption)
key_assumptions.supported_by: The wage projections predict control-group respondents' actual re-employment wages nearly one-to-one (Figure 1, Coef = 1.049, SE = 0.036); strong first-stage effects on expected wage offers

key_assumptions.assumption: Treatment effects on survey-reported outcomes reflect genuine belief updating rather than numerical anchoring on the presented number or experimenter demand effects
key_assumptions.supported_by: Effects on expected wage offers largely persist in a follow-up survey one to two weeks later (Appendix Figure A.6); the neutral group, whose beliefs are confirmed, shows no revision

threats_discussed: Perception gaps are not randomly assigned, so differential treatment effects across prior-belief groups could reflect other group characteristics or differences in information processing rather than prior beliefs (Appendix Tables A.2 and A.6)
Numerical anchoring on the presented information and experimenter demand effects in survey-based outcomes (addressed with the follow-up survey)
Differential selection into employment when comparing realized hourly wages (addressed with within-worker wage changes and Lee (2009) bounds)
Multiple hypothesis testing across the many outcomes (addressed with sharpened q-values)
robustness_checks: Alternative perception-gap thresholds of 10%, 12.5%, 17.5% and 20% instead of +/-15% (Appendix Figure A.10)
Alternative winsorization at the 1st and 99th percentiles (Appendix Table A.8)
Exclusion of respondents who were previously part-time employed (Appendix Table A.10)
Sharpened false-discovery-rate q-values for multiple hypothesis testing (Anderson, 2008) (Appendix Table A.9)
Sequentially adding interactions of the treatment indicator with background characteristics, to separate perception-gap size from differential information processing (Appendix Table A.6)
Alternative specification interacting the treatment with the continuous perception gap on the full sample (Appendix Table A.7, equation 2)
Correlational analysis of perception gaps within the control group, expected to have the opposite sign (Appendix Table A.5)
Persistence of belief effects in a follow-up survey one to two weeks later (Appendix Figure A.6)
unresolved_confounders: The asymmetry between responses to positive and negative shocks cannot be attributed to shock direction versus systematic differences between the groups receiving positive and negative updates ('respondents' perception gaps are not randomly assigned')
General-equilibrium effects of a large-scale roll-out (crowding-out versus improved matching) are not assessed

estimation.specification: OLS of Expected wage offered (log) on the treatment indicator within the prior-perception-gap group, controlling for the baseline covariates listed in Table 1; robust standard errors. The paper prints no estimating equation for this specification.

treatment.label: Information treatment: randomized provision of the actual average monthly re-employment wage of comparable workers (large positive prior perception gap (log) > +0.15 (initially highly pessimistic))

register_source.value: Danish labor market registers covering all unemployed job seekers re-employed between 2013 and 2022, used to compute the cell-level wage projection; no register code or variable name is stated

definition.value: Binary indicator for being in the randomly selected half of main-survey respondents who were shown, in text and in a bar chart, the actual average monthly re-employment wage (before taxes, excluding pension contributions) of job seekers in their own demographic cell; the control group received no information. The effect is estimated separately within each prior-perception-gap group, so in this group the treatment delivers a large positive information shock (the signal exceeds the prior belief by more than 15%).

timing.value: Delivered during the main online survey (fielded from 23 October 2023), after elicitation of prior beliefs about comparable workers' re-employment wages and before elicitation of expected wage offers, reservation wages and search outcomes

register_source.value: Register data from Statistics Denmark on respondents' labor market outcomes (monthly employment status, working hours, labor earnings, occupation as reported by employers); no register code or variable name is given

definition.value: Total working hours accumulated over the six months after the intervention, observed in administrative records; winsorized at the 95th percentile

timing.value: Cumulated over the six months following the intervention

units.value: working hours accumulated over six months

magnitude.interpretation: an 11.1% rise in total working hours (p = 0.069)

estimand.target_population: Main-survey respondents with a large positive prior perception gap (log) in (+0.150;+infinity], i.e. job seekers who initially underestimated the average re-employment wage of comparable workers by more than 15% (initially highly pessimistic)
estimand.time_horizon: Cumulated over six months after the intervention
estimand.formal_query: E[Total hours 6m. | do(information provided)] - E[Total hours 6m. | do(no information)] for respondents with a large positive prior perception gap (log) > +0.15 (initially highly pessimistic)

population.description: Main-survey respondents with a large positive prior perception gap (log) in (+0.150;+infinity], i.e. job seekers who initially underestimated the average re-employment wage of comparable workers by more than 15% (initially highly pessimistic); N = 1,723 in this estimation
population.ages: Working-age unemployment benefit recipients (age groups: 35 or below, 36-50, above 50)
population.period: Main survey fielded from 23 October 2023 for about five weeks; administrative outcomes followed up to six months after the survey
subgroups_defined: pre-treatment search radius below vs. above ten kilometres (local vs. distant job seekers)
population.selection: Voluntary respondents to a survey invitation sent through Denmark's official digital government mailing system to all registered unemployment benefit recipients as of 23 October 2023 (13,234 completed the main survey, a 15.8% response rate); respondents who had already accepted a job, sought only part-time work, had never been employed or belonged to a register cell with fewer than 30 observations were excluded, as were the top and bottom percentiles of response time

identification.source_of_variation: Random assignment of a random half of main-survey respondents to receive information on the actual average monthly re-employment wage of job seekers in their own demographic cell (survey information-provision experiment fielded from 23 October 2023)

key_assumptions.assumption: Random assignment of the information treatment: within each prior-belief group, treatment status is independent of respondents' potential outcomes and background characteristics, so the treatment-control difference identifies the causal effect of receiving the wage information
key_assumptions.supported_by: Balance tests in Table 1 (treatment-control p-values and joint F-tests of 0.90 for the main and 0.76 for the follow-up sample); Appendix Table A.2 reports characteristics by perception-gap group

rhs: Potential outcomes and baseline characteristics of the respondent

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference between respondents: one respondent's treatment status does not affect another respondent's search behaviour or labour market outcomes (no crowding-out in the vacancy market)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Not tested; the paper notes that assessing the welfare implications of a large-scale roll-out would require accounting for general-equilibrium effects

key_assumptions.assumption: Job seekers regard the re-employment wages of comparable workers as informative for their own wage prospects (the design's explicitly testable assumption)
key_assumptions.supported_by: The wage projections predict control-group respondents' actual re-employment wages nearly one-to-one (Figure 1, Coef = 1.049, SE = 0.036); strong first-stage effects on expected wage offers

threats_discussed: Perception gaps are not randomly assigned, so differential treatment effects across prior-belief groups could reflect other group characteristics or differences in information processing rather than prior beliefs (Appendix Tables A.2 and A.6)
Numerical anchoring on the presented information and experimenter demand effects in survey-based outcomes (addressed with the follow-up survey)
Differential selection into employment when comparing realized hourly wages (addressed with within-worker wage changes and Lee (2009) bounds)
Multiple hypothesis testing across the many outcomes (addressed with sharpened q-values)
robustness_checks: Alternative perception-gap thresholds of 10%, 12.5%, 17.5% and 20% instead of +/-15% (Appendix Figure A.10)
Alternative winsorization at the 1st and 99th percentiles (Appendix Table A.8)
Exclusion of respondents who were previously part-time employed (Appendix Table A.10)
Sharpened false-discovery-rate q-values for multiple hypothesis testing (Anderson, 2008) (Appendix Table A.9)
Sequentially adding interactions of the treatment indicator with background characteristics, to separate perception-gap size from differential information processing (Appendix Table A.6)
Alternative specification interacting the treatment with the continuous perception gap on the full sample (Appendix Table A.7, equation 2)
Correlational analysis of perception gaps within the control group, expected to have the opposite sign (Appendix Table A.5)
Persistence of belief effects in a follow-up survey one to two weeks later (Appendix Figure A.6)
unresolved_confounders: The asymmetry between responses to positive and negative shocks cannot be attributed to shock direction versus systematic differences between the groups receiving positive and negative updates ('respondents' perception gaps are not randomly assigned')
General-equilibrium effects of a large-scale roll-out (crowding-out versus improved matching) are not assessed

estimation.specification: OLS of Total hours 6m. on the treatment indicator within the prior-perception-gap group, controlling for the baseline covariates listed in Table 1; robust standard errors. The paper prints no estimating equation for this specification.

treatment.label: Information treatment: randomized provision of the actual average monthly re-employment wage of comparable workers (large positive prior perception gap (log) > +0.15 (initially highly pessimistic))

register_source.value: Danish labor market registers covering all unemployed job seekers re-employed between 2013 and 2022, used to compute the cell-level wage projection; no register code or variable name is stated

definition.value: Binary indicator for being in the randomly selected half of main-survey respondents who were shown, in text and in a bar chart, the actual average monthly re-employment wage (before taxes, excluding pension contributions) of job seekers in their own demographic cell; the control group received no information. The effect is estimated separately within each prior-perception-gap group, so in this group the treatment delivers a large positive information shock (the signal exceeds the prior belief by more than 15%).

timing.value: Delivered during the main online survey (fielded from 23 October 2023), after elicitation of prior beliefs about comparable workers' re-employment wages and before elicitation of expected wage offers, reservation wages and search outcomes

register_source.value: Register data from Statistics Denmark on respondents' labor market outcomes (monthly employment status, working hours, labor earnings, occupation as reported by employers); no register code or variable name is given

definition.value: Average monthly employment rate over the six months after the intervention, observed in administrative records

timing.value: Six months following the intervention

units.value: share (average monthly employment rate; the table header labels it in percentage points, so a coefficient of 0.01 = 1 pp)

estimand.target_population: Main-survey respondents with a large positive prior perception gap (log) in (+0.150;+infinity], i.e. job seekers who initially underestimated the average re-employment wage of comparable workers by more than 15% (initially highly pessimistic), split by pre-treatment search radius (local searchers)
estimand.time_horizon: Average over the six months after the intervention
estimand.formal_query: E[Empl. rate 6m. (pp.) | do(information provided)] - E[Empl. rate 6m. (pp.) | do(no information)] for respondents with a large positive prior perception gap (log) > +0.15 (initially highly pessimistic)

population.description: Main-survey respondents with a large positive prior perception gap (log) in (+0.150;+infinity], i.e. job seekers who initially underestimated the average re-employment wage of comparable workers by more than 15% (initially highly pessimistic); estimates by pre-treatment search radius, this coefficient refers to local searchers (radius below ten kilometres); N = 1,453 in the pooled estimation
population.ages: Working-age unemployment benefit recipients (age groups: 35 or below, 36-50, above 50)
population.period: Main survey fielded from 23 October 2023 for about five weeks; administrative outcomes followed up to six months after the survey
subgroups_defined: pre-treatment search radius below vs. above ten kilometres (local vs. distant job seekers)
population.selection: Voluntary respondents to a survey invitation sent through Denmark's official digital government mailing system to all registered unemployment benefit recipients as of 23 October 2023 (13,234 completed the main survey, a 15.8% response rate); respondents who had already accepted a job, sought only part-time work, had never been employed or belonged to a register cell with fewer than 30 observations were excluded, as were the top and bottom percentiles of response time

identification.source_of_variation: Random assignment of a random half of main-survey respondents to receive information on the actual average monthly re-employment wage of job seekers in their own demographic cell (survey information-provision experiment fielded from 23 October 2023)

key_assumptions.assumption: Random assignment of the information treatment: within each prior-belief group, treatment status is independent of respondents' potential outcomes and background characteristics, so the treatment-control difference identifies the causal effect of receiving the wage information
key_assumptions.supported_by: Balance tests in Table 1 (treatment-control p-values and joint F-tests of 0.90 for the main and 0.76 for the follow-up sample); Appendix Table A.2 reports characteristics by perception-gap group

rhs: Potential outcomes and baseline characteristics of the respondent

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference between respondents: one respondent's treatment status does not affect another respondent's search behaviour or labour market outcomes (no crowding-out in the vacancy market)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Not tested; the paper notes that assessing the welfare implications of a large-scale roll-out would require accounting for general-equilibrium effects

key_assumptions.assumption: Job seekers regard the re-employment wages of comparable workers as informative for their own wage prospects (the design's explicitly testable assumption)
key_assumptions.supported_by: The wage projections predict control-group respondents' actual re-employment wages nearly one-to-one (Figure 1, Coef = 1.049, SE = 0.036); strong first-stage effects on expected wage offers

threats_discussed: Perception gaps are not randomly assigned, so differential treatment effects across prior-belief groups could reflect other group characteristics or differences in information processing rather than prior beliefs (Appendix Tables A.2 and A.6)
Numerical anchoring on the presented information and experimenter demand effects in survey-based outcomes (addressed with the follow-up survey)
Differential selection into employment when comparing realized hourly wages (addressed with within-worker wage changes and Lee (2009) bounds)
Multiple hypothesis testing across the many outcomes (addressed with sharpened q-values)
robustness_checks: Alternative perception-gap thresholds of 10%, 12.5%, 17.5% and 20% instead of +/-15% (Appendix Figure A.10)
Alternative winsorization at the 1st and 99th percentiles (Appendix Table A.8)
Exclusion of respondents who were previously part-time employed (Appendix Table A.10)
Sharpened false-discovery-rate q-values for multiple hypothesis testing (Anderson, 2008) (Appendix Table A.9)
Sequentially adding interactions of the treatment indicator with background characteristics, to separate perception-gap size from differential information processing (Appendix Table A.6)
Alternative specification interacting the treatment with the continuous perception gap on the full sample (Appendix Table A.7, equation 2)
Correlational analysis of perception gaps within the control group, expected to have the opposite sign (Appendix Table A.5)
Persistence of belief effects in a follow-up survey one to two weeks later (Appendix Figure A.6)
unresolved_confounders: The asymmetry between responses to positive and negative shocks cannot be attributed to shock direction versus systematic differences between the groups receiving positive and negative updates ('respondents' perception gaps are not randomly assigned')
General-equilibrium effects of a large-scale roll-out (crowding-out versus improved matching) are not assessed

identification.source_of_variation: Random assignment of a random half of main-survey respondents to receive information on the actual average monthly re-employment wage of job seekers in their own demographic cell (survey information-provision experiment fielded from 23 October 2023)

key_assumptions.assumption: Random assignment of the information treatment: within each prior-belief group, treatment status is independent of respondents' potential outcomes and background characteristics, so the treatment-control difference identifies the causal effect of receiving the wage information
key_assumptions.supported_by: Balance tests in Table 1 (treatment-control p-values and joint F-tests of 0.90 for the main and 0.76 for the follow-up sample); Appendix Table A.2 reports characteristics by perception-gap group

rhs: Potential outcomes and baseline characteristics of the respondent

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference between respondents: one respondent's treatment status does not affect another respondent's search behaviour or labour market outcomes (no crowding-out in the vacancy market)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Not tested; the paper notes that assessing the welfare implications of a large-scale roll-out would require accounting for general-equilibrium effects

implies_edges.to: Likelihood of applying outside one's own region within four weeks after the survey (pp.)

key_assumptions.assumption: Job seekers regard the re-employment wages of comparable workers as informative for their own wage prospects (the design's explicitly testable assumption)
key_assumptions.supported_by: The wage projections predict control-group respondents' actual re-employment wages nearly one-to-one (Figure 1, Coef = 1.049, SE = 0.036); strong first-stage effects on expected wage offers

threats_discussed: Perception gaps are not randomly assigned, so differential treatment effects across prior-belief groups could reflect other group characteristics or differences in information processing rather than prior beliefs (Appendix Tables A.2 and A.6)
Numerical anchoring on the presented information and experimenter demand effects in survey-based outcomes (addressed with the follow-up survey)
Differential selection into employment when comparing realized hourly wages (addressed with within-worker wage changes and Lee (2009) bounds)
Multiple hypothesis testing across the many outcomes (addressed with sharpened q-values)
robustness_checks: Alternative perception-gap thresholds of 10%, 12.5%, 17.5% and 20% instead of +/-15% (Appendix Figure A.10)
Alternative winsorization at the 1st and 99th percentiles (Appendix Table A.8)
Exclusion of respondents who were previously part-time employed (Appendix Table A.10)
Sharpened false-discovery-rate q-values for multiple hypothesis testing (Anderson, 2008) (Appendix Table A.9)
Sequentially adding interactions of the treatment indicator with background characteristics, to separate perception-gap size from differential information processing (Appendix Table A.6)
Alternative specification interacting the treatment with the continuous perception gap on the full sample (Appendix Table A.7, equation 2)
Correlational analysis of perception gaps within the control group, expected to have the opposite sign (Appendix Table A.5)
Persistence of belief effects in a follow-up survey one to two weeks later (Appendix Figure A.6)
unresolved_confounders: The asymmetry between responses to positive and negative shocks cannot be attributed to shock direction versus systematic differences between the groups receiving positive and negative updates ('respondents' perception gaps are not randomly assigned')
General-equilibrium effects of a large-scale roll-out (crowding-out versus improved matching) are not assessed
